prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, opening a new regime of precision timekeeping.

statement.case_for: Reading the eight opening ballots, the optical lattice clock is the one candidate that holds up on every axis I weigh. It is a clear invention with a precise, checkable outcome: the magic-wavelength idea cancels the light shift that would otherwise ruin a trapped-atom clock, and the resulting clocks reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It was ranked in the top three by six of eight members and first by three, and the support is not just numerical. Every colleague who assessed it describes the same two-part attribution, Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the frontier, which gives a clean two-person configuration. The performance has been reproduced by many independent laboratories and species and compared across continents, so the interpretation is stable and the science is mature. It also fits what I said publicly about the criterion, that the prize is for a discovery or invention rather than a lifetime of work (as reported by Tohoku University): this is an invention that did something its predecessors could not. Its consequences, tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the pending redefinition of the second, are concrete and growing. My own first choice, aberration correction, was supported by nobody else, and I take that as real information rather than something to argue around.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with prizes already given. Hall and Haensch (2005) for the frequency comb and Wineland and Haroche (2012) for ion control mean the committee could judge that the territory is already substantially honoured, and the optical lattice clock a refinement of that lineage. Attribution is also less settled than a two-name list suggests: Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Takamoto and other groups contributed important lattice-clock results, and the early proposal history has additional contributors that the supplied credit does not capture. Finally, the formal redefinition of the SI second has not happened, so some of the practical impact is still prospective. I think these points qualify the case rather than defeat it, because the lattice clock is a distinct scheme and the accuracy it delivered was a step change, but they should be argued out rather than assumed away.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a simple, original idea whose laser-spectroscopy and coherence control are mature, with Katori making the decisive proposal and Ye's group driving record accuracy; he also notes the 2005 comb prize may lead some members to see the topic as partly recognised, and he has not verified current best uncertainties or other early contributors.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with the maturity judgement, and I share his worry about 2005. My answer to it is that the comb was a ruler for optical frequencies and the lattice clock is a different invention: a way of holding many neutral atoms with the perturbation engineered away. That distinction is the sort the committee can document by looking at the origin of the 1e-18 results. What I would still like us to check, since neither of us has, is the early-proposal record, so that Katori is credited for the right step and the citation does not over-reach.

responses.point: Danielsson places the Higgs boson observation by ATLAS and CMS first, arguing that the experimental discovery was never recognised after the 2013 theory prize and that the founders Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee give a defensible three-person configuration, while conceding that it is leadership credit and not discovery-day credit and that many analysts sit outside the trio.
responses.response: I accept that the science is beyond doubt and that the discovery is overdue, and I do not dismiss it. My disagreement is about what the three names stand for. The criterion as I understand it is to identify the topic and the people responsible for the original work. Danielsson himself says the trio represents institutional leadership of the detectors and not the discovery analysis, and Pearce, Eriksson and Kroll make the same point. If the committee honours detector founders, the citation has to say so honestly, and then it is a prize for building instruments, which is a coherent choice but not the one the discovery framing implies. I would put the lattice clock ahead because its credit maps onto two named people and an identifiable idea, while I would keep B057 open as the main rival and want to hear how he would word the citation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a predicted flat-band condition (Bistritzer and MacDonald) followed by the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity (Jarillo-Herrero), a tunable platform with broad impact, replicated widely though the pairing mechanism is still debated.
responses.response: I put this fifth, and I find his case for the theory-plus-experiment pairing persuasive as an attribution. Where I differ is on timing. Several colleagues, including Pearce, Eriksson and Kroll, point out that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and reproducibility depends on sample quality and twist-angle disorder. In my own experience with oxide interfaces, a result that depends strongly on sample-to-sample structure deserves patience before we cite it as settled. I would not exclude it, and it is my first alternative, but I think waiting a few years costs little and the lattice clock has no comparable open question.

responses.point: Johansson ranks trapped-ion quantum computing first (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) as the foundation of hardware quantum computing and the seed of analogue simulation, while acknowledging overlap with the 2012 Wineland prize and that the entry bundles quantum computing with cold-atom simulation; he also flags his own Chalmers and WACQT connections to the circuit QED community.
responses.response: I respect that he declared his connection, and I should do the same: we are both at Chalmers, so I will not treat his support for circuit QED, or his assessment of it, as independent of that setting, and I would ask the same caution of myself. On the substance, I think his own reservations are the right ones. The B038 entry bundles distinct achievements, ion gates and cold-atom simulation, and 2012 already honoured ion control, so the prize would have to be narrowed before I could support it. If the committee prefers a quantum-information prize I would sooner look at the clean three-name Bennett, Brassard and Ekert configuration that we both ranked in the top three.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first as the organising framework for correlated electrons, but notes that the infinite-dimension limit is usually credited to Metzner and Vollhardt, that Metzner is not among the credited names, and that DFT+DMFT depends on double-counting and interaction-parameter choices.
responses.response: His own attribution caveat is, to my mind, decisive for this round. A prize whose foundational step is credited to someone we cannot name, and which he himself calls a method as much as a discovery, is hard to defend as a clean configuration. I do value the framework, because it is the theory I would reach for when comparing spectroscopy to calculation, and I would not want this exchange to count as a verdict on its merit. I would ask him whether the committee could instead cite the concept and the impurity mapping in a way that fits the three credited names, and if not, I think this stays on the list but not in the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make a lattice-clock prize look like too small a step beyond already honoured work.
Exact early-proposal and first-demonstration priority among Katori and other lattice-clock groups, which none of the openings verified in detail.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second before awarding.
How far the committee should go in crediting detector founders for B057, and what that choice would imply for the discovery criterion.
Whether the pairing mechanism and sample dependence in magic-angle graphene will settle in the coming years.
statement.conflict_note: Two connections should be recorded. First, my first-ranked ballot B028 (aberration correction in electron microscopy) is in my own research field of transmission electron microscopy, and I have led the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so I should recuse myself from deliberating on it and I have not made it my preferred configuration. Second, my profile lists a University of Tokyo fellowship, a JSPS fellowship and long-running exchanges with Japanese universities, and Katori is at Japanese institutions; no personal or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye is documented, so I see no specific conflict for B042, but I flag the connection for the committee to judge. Goran Johansson, who is also at Chalmers, has a stated interest in B049, and I have no direct tie to that candidate.
